items.title: I made dinner. It made the post.
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

I recorded a 47-second clip asking for a reel. Then I went and started dinner.

While the water was heating up, the thing cut the video, wrote the captions, checked it for anything it shouldn't put out, and posted it to Instagram.

It went live at 4:44. I was in the kitchen. Nobody was in the room.

Here's the part I keep chewing on: I didn't get faster. I got removed. The bottleneck was never the editing or the uploading â€” it was me, deciding to sit down and do it.

Most of what I call being busy is just me being the only one who can do the thing.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: The devil's weapon is ambivalence
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

The devil doesn't need to ruin your life. He just needs you to wait.

Napoleon Hill wrote about this in Outwitting the Devil â€” he figured 98% of people are drifters. Not bad people. Just people who never quite decided, and handed the choice over to circumstances instead.

Then the hesitating hardens. He called it hypnotic rhythm: indecision stops being a moment and becomes the default setting.

Here's the part that got me. You're not delaying a choice. You're conditioning yourself to be paralyzed.

So whatever you've been sitting on â€” it is costing you more to not decide than it would cost you to decide wrong and move.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: Money is not the root of all evil
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

"Money is the root of all evil." A friend said it to me today, and I want to squash it â€” because I think that sentence quietly stops a lot of good people from ever going after what they want.

Money is a modality. It's a tool. It's how we measure value moving through the world.

It amplifies whatever you're already holding. So yes â€” it will magnify evil that was already in there. That's not the same as causing it.

Here's the question worth sitting with: did evil exist before money did?

If it did, then money can't be the root of it.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

And I said on camera I'd make you the getting-started list. It's done â€” eight steps, in order, free, no signup, nothing to hand over. It's on my site, sheet 03.

items.title: The wrong decision beats indecision
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

The wrong decision beats indecision. Not as a motivational line â€” as a metabolic one.

Dr. Martin Picard studies mitochondria at Columbia. The short version: everything costs energy, including the things you don't do. Sitting in ambivalence isn't free. It's expensive.

One honest caveat, and I say it in the video too â€” I'm recalling the number from memory and I could be off. Take the figure as my recollection, not a citation. The direction is the part I'd stake something on.

So decide. You can correct a wrong turn. You can't correct a car that never left the driveway.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

Nothing clever about it. It just means the six-month tighten-up actually happens, because the excuse is gone.

items.title: Give the value away
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

I see folks out on the corners holding signs. And I see clients, and I see patients, doing a version of the same thing.

Here's what I think they have in common, and I'm including myself in this. Every single person is holding something valuable. And we keep it tight. We keep it buried where nobody can get at it.

That's the mistake. Not that you don't have anything worth giving â€” that you're sitting on it.

So give it away. Give, give, give. That's the part I'm still working on.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: God-sized goals â€” the not-knowing is the point
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

If you already know how to reach it, it isn't a goal. It's a task.

I heard Dan Martell describe carrying goals so big he has no idea how he'd pull them off â€” and that the size is the whole point. Big enough that his ceiling ends up being somebody else's floor.

The part that got me wasn't the ambition. It was what comes after: you have to hand it over. Not the plan â€” you don't have a plan. The not-knowing.

I've spent years treating "I don't know how" as a reason to shrink the goal back down to something I could picture. He's saying that's backwards. Not knowing how is the evidence you finally picked a real one.

So pick the one you can't figure out yet. Then stop trying to figure it out before you start.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: Just-in-case people vs just-in-time people
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

There are just-in-case people and there are just-in-time people.

Just-in-case waits until he's sure. One more book, one more course, one more year of getting ready â€” waiting to become the guy who'd be qualified to start.

Just-in-time moves, and works it out on the way down.

I was just-in-case for a long time and I called it being responsible. It wasn't. It was fear with a respectable job title.

Here's the part nobody mentions: the certainty you're waiting on doesn't show up before the action. It shows up because of it.

Wrong action, messy action, or a slam dunk â€” matters far less than moving. You can steer something that's rolling. You can't steer something parked.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

Open your calendar before noon and delete one recurring thing. Just one. That's addition by subtraction.

items.title: The bird and the twig (NF)
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

I was patching walls in my son's room, listening to his music â€” an artist called NF â€” and one idea wouldn't let go.

I'll brutalize the quote, and I say so in the video too. It goes something like this: do you know why a bird perches on a twig? Is it because it trusts the twig to hold its weight? Or because it trusts its own ability to fly away?

Most of us spend our lives testing twigs. Checking if the job is safe, if the market is safe, if the timing is safe.

The bird doesn't audit the twig. It knows what its wings can do.

Think about that.

items.title: Willpower is finite â€” the Swiss cheese model
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

The gift bags called me out. There WAS a system â€” and it's broken, because it ran on willpower.

A system that relies on willpower is bound to break. Willpower is finite. One bad day, one bad week, and the energy that was holding the whole thing together is gone.

So you don't build one perfect layer. You build layers, plural. In medicine it's called the Swiss cheese model: every layer has holes, but you stack them so the holes don't line up. More layers, fewer things get through â€” and when something breaks, it's an easy fix instead of a collapse.

Stop blaming your discipline. Start stacking layers.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

items.title: Every system dies at 3 months
items.caption:

The fix isn't a better system. It's a standing appointment with the system: a quarterly meeting to re-inspire it, spot what's about to break, and fix it while it's still cheap to fix.

Put the check-up on the calendar before you need it.

So now they get the list instead. Backpack? Glove? Bat? Shoes - because you don't want sand in there and you want to run fast.

items.title: The Alchemist - beginner's luck isn't luck
items.caption:
Hey Dad,

Storytime. The Alchemist, page 54.

The merchant tells the boy business is good - soon you'll be able to go back to your sheep. Why ask more out of life? And the boy answers before he means to: because we have to respond to omens.

Then he regrets saying it, because the merchant never met the king.

Coelho calls it the principle of favorability. Beginner's luck. Life tilts toward you at the start because it wants you to go after your personal legend.

Here's my read on it. Even when it doesn't feel like a lesson, it's refinement. It's preparing you for the next one - the next opportunity in your life's true purpose.

And the part I keep coming back to: the more you succeed, the more the rest of the world succeeds.

So go get it.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.

Accept yourself, and you'll find yourself surrounded by people who accept you too. And watch what happens to the people who required you to be someone else.

We're all part of one big, beautiful ocean. One molecule colliding with another moves the next one. It's a wave. (You love water analogies. I love water analogies.)

So â€” you're not alone. And if hearing that stings a little, that twinge is a signal. There's a rumor in your mind worth dispelling. I want you to win, because the more free you feel, the more it ripples to the rest of us.

Not because of one decision. Because I built — the way most people build — an environment where drifting was just far too easy. Nothing dramatic. Easy is the whole danger.

And I'm sorry. To a lot of people, and to myself, for those years.

Because it looks to me like my impact could have been much greater, much sooner. And a lot of pain could have been avoided — at minimum in my life, and in the lives of the people standing closest to me.

I'm not telling you this for sympathy. I'm telling you because the drift is quiet while it's happening, and somebody has to say that out loud.

Lead with intention. Keep your purpose in mind. You will not be subject to drifting.

Thanks, Dad. I love you, Dad.
